slides.body: Hotel Brendle is home base — for the folks who live here, the guests passing through, and the Robstown neighbors who’ve watched over this corner for generations.

slides.title: Welcome in, neighbors

slides.body: The Brendle runs on neighbors looking out for each other. Start at the front desk — if we can’t help, we’ll point you to someone local who can.

bullets.text: New around here? Introduce yourself at the front desk. Around the Brendle, folks know each other by name — that’s the point of the place.
Missing something? Keys, glasses, a jacket left in the lobby — check lost & found at the front desk. Found something? Bring it by.
Got a notice to share? A ride, a yard sale, a job lead, a church supper — ask at the front desk about sharing it with the house.

bullets.text: by C.C. Brendle and V.V. Elick, at the junction of the Texas-Mexican and the St. Louis, Brownsville & Mexico railroads — right here at 601 East Avenue A, Robstown.
The hotel opened its doors with 36 rooms for railroad travelers.
Brick parapet, red tile roof on brackets, and a semi-circular arch over the doorway.
Recorded Texas Historic Landmark marker, designated 1984.
The hotel passed to the Sons of Hermann, who kept it standing through hard times.
Robstown is the birthplace of Texas Hold’em — recognized by the Texas Legislature in 2007.

slides.body: Robstown began about 1906 at the junction of two railroads — the Texas-Mexican and the St. Louis, Brownsville & Mexico. The hotel opened in 1914 right at that junction, and freight trains still roll past the hotel today.

bullets.text: Robstown was founded at the crossing of the Texas-Mexican and the St. Louis, Brownsville & Mexico railroads — the town grew up around the tracks.
The crossing east of the hotel is still managed as Tower 197. A connector track sends Laredo trains north on Union Pacific’s line toward Houston.

Freight still runs through Robstown on Union Pacific tracks, with Canadian Pacific Kansas City — the old Texas-Mexican line — running trains through on trackage rights. More trains are planned on the Robstown–Beaumont line.
Look northeast from the hotel — the water tower on the skyline is Robstown’s landmark, standing over the town the railroads built.

slides.foot: Sources: Handbook of Texas (TSHA), Texas Railroad History — Tower 197, Texas Historical Commission Marker No. 22460 (2019) · Nov 7, 2026
slides.note: Water tower: its height, date, and lettering could not be confirmed in public sources this round, so the slide only points guests to look northeast — per the hotel’s own site notes. The Oct 2024 tank collapse south of Robstown was a ground storage tank, not this tower, and was left out.

slides.body: A real WWII aircraft carrier turned museum, docked on North Beach in Corpus Christi — about 22 miles east of the hotel, roughly 25 minutes by car. Open today, Saturday, 9:00 AM – 5:00 PM.

bullets.text: Explore the flight deck, hangar deck, bridge, and vintage aircraft aboard the “Blue Ghost,” plus a 3D theater. A flight simulator is available for an extra fee.
Adults $25, seniors $21, military $16 with ID, youth 13–17 $20, children 4–12 $15, under 3 free. Parking $5 all day. Tickets at the ship — not sold online.
Veterans, active duty, and Reservists get in free today, Saturday Nov 7 — and Nov 8 and Nov 11 — for Veterans Day weekend.
2914 N Shoreline Blvd, Corpus Christi. Phone (361) 888-4873, usslexington.com.

bullets.text: Keep the shared spaces welcoming. The lobby, halls, and porch belong to everybody here — leave them ready for the next neighbor.
Look out for each other. Hold the door, share what you know about town, and check in on a neighbor who’s been quiet.
Bring it to the front desk. Need a hand, have a concern, or see something that needs fixing? The front desk is the first stop — day or evening.

slides.body: Our restoration series: one fix per video — the problem, the repair, and the finished result, filmed right here. Robstown gets to watch its landmark come back, one fix at a time.
slides.foot: Every episode ends the same way: “Be careful kids, have fun.”
